Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative unfolds primarily through vivid, real-time scenes—the drive to the beach, the picnic with the wine bottle, walking along the shore, wading back through the rising tide, and the quiet drive home. These scenes feature engaging dialogue and small physical actions that dramatize the unspoken romantic tension between Marian and Anton. 

Woven seamlessly into these scenes are brief moments of summary and exposition that compress the previous five weeks of the residency and provide essential context without slowing down the pace. For instance, the narrator uses summary to describe how Marian has come to know Anton's face over five weeks, the logistics of their upcoming departures, the memory of the power cut three weeks earlier, and the crucial exposition that Anton has a wife in Rotterdam. The story also utilizes forward-looking summary near the end (imagining the final dinner and packing) to underscore the fleeting nature of their time together, before grounding the reader back in the final scene in the car. This interplay makes the present-day scenes emotionally resonant while efficiently delivering the necessary backstory.
